opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's a really interesting question, and honestly something I've thought about a lot.

Part of it is just that Singapore is a pretty natural hub. It's well connected, it's safe, it's English-speaking, and it's a place where people from across Southeast Asia, and even further, like India, China, or Australia, can see themselves living. A lot of strong researchers in the region historically felt they had to go to the Bay Area or London to do frontier work. If you can offer that same kind of work closer to home, that's a very compelling pitch.

The bigger thing, though, is the work itself. Talented people want to work on hard problems with real compute and real impact. They don't want a satellite office doing peripheral stuff. So I've always tried to make sure the team in Singapore is doing core work, the kind of thing that ends up in the main models. Once people see that, the location stops being a compromise and becomes a bonus.

There's also a bit of a personal element. I'm from Singapore, and I've been fortunate to work in the Bay Area and with folks all over. I think there's a lot of latent talent in this part of the world that just hasn't had the opportunities. Some of the best people I've worked with came from nontraditional paths. They didn't have the fanciest pedigree, but they were extremely hungry and really good engineers. So a lot of it is being willing to look in places other people aren't looking and betting on people early.

And talent attracts talent. Once you get a few really strong people, the next hires come much more easily, because people want to work with people they respect. Building that initial core is the hardest part, but after that it kind of compounds.

r001.rationale: The response says the speaker helped ensure the Singapore team did core work, but it does not mention Quoc or attribute recruiting regional AI talent to involvement of Yi Tay and Quoc’s team.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few things going on. The first is just that, honestly, I'm Singaporean, and I came back here to build Reka after being at Google Brain for a number of years, so there's a bit of a personal angle to it. And I think when people see that someone who's done frontier work at a place like Google decides to come back and do it from Singapore, that signals that it's actually possible. You don't have to be in the Bay Area to train large models or do serious research.

The second thing is that Southeast Asia and the broader region have a lot of really strong technical people who, for various reasons, don't want to or can't move to the US. Visa issues are a real thing. Family is a real thing. Singapore is a few hours' flight from basically everywhere in the region, it's English-speaking, it's stable, and it's a place where a lot of people from Indonesia, Malaysia, Vietnam, India, China are already comfortable being. So we're kind of a natural landing spot for people who want to work on frontier stuff but stay close to home.

And then I'd say the third thing is just the work itself. Talent follows interesting problems. If you're actually training models from scratch, doing pretraining, doing the hard infra stuff, people who care about that will find you. We've had people reach out because they read a paper or saw something we shipped and they just wanted to be part of a team doing real model training rather than wrapping an API. That matters a lot more than location, to be honest. If the work is boring, being in San Francisco doesn't save you.

The flip side is it's still a small ecosystem compared to the Bay Area. There's less of a dense network of people who've done this before, so a lot of it is us bringing that know-how and training people up. But I actually kind of like that. There's a lot of untapped potential here, and I think over the next few years you'll see more of it.

r001.rationale: The response credits Yi Tay’s return to Singapore and his work building Reka, but it does not mention Quoc or attribute recruitment to Quoc’s team.

astra-6.text:
I think Singapore is an attractive place for people in the region to come and work. But for AI talent, the bigger question is: what do you actually get to work on? Do you get to tackle ambitious research problems? Do you get to work with people you can learn from? Do you have the resources to pursue your ideas?

So I think our ability to attract people depends on building that kind of environment. If someone wants to work at the frontier, we want them to see a path to doing that here, without feeling that they have to move to the US. Location helps, but ultimately it's the work and the team that make people want to join—and stay.

r001.rationale: The response says Singapore’s ability to attract talent depends on the work, resources, and team environment, but it does not attribute recruitment to Yi Tay and Quoc’s team specifically.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a lot of talent in the region, and Singapore is a very attractive place for people to come and work. But ultimately, you have to give them an interesting problem to work on. If someone wants to work on frontier models, can they do that here? Can they work with a strong team, get access to compute, and have ownership over something meaningful? That’s the opportunity we want to create.

I also think there’s something compelling about being able to do this closer to home. People shouldn’t necessarily have to move to the US to pursue their ambitions in AI. But we still have to earn their interest through the quality of the work and the team.

r001.rationale: The response discusses Singapore’s appeal and the team’s efforts to attract talent, but it does not identify Yi Tay and Quoc’s team as the reason for the ability to recruit regional AI talent.
